title: Development, performance and use of landscape indicators of resilience and resistance—A response to Applestein and Germino (2025)
content:
Landscape R&R indicators have performed well at large landscape scales and been used successfully to develop management strategies and prioritizations for the sagebrush biome and south-west drylands. Products derived from the indicators are being used to develop appropriate management strategies for large-scale planning areas. Appropriate use of the indicators, as shown here, requires understanding the relevant metrics and using properly scaled data.


Abstract

Concepts of ecological resilience to disturbance and resistance to invasion (R&R) are widely used across shrublands and woodlands of the western United States to characterize likely responses to disturbances and management actions. Landscape-scale indicators of R&R were developed to operationalize these concepts. An attempt to use the landscape R&R indicators to explain plant-community recovery at plot scales after wildfires, that is, Applestein & Germino (2025), indicated the need to explain the development, performance and use of the indicators. Landscape indicators of R&R provide quantitative insight into an area's potential to recover from disturbances and resist annual grass invasion that can be generalized and applied across space and time. Factors like residual vegetation, weather and management influence responses to disturbances and can result in different successional stages and plant community compositions (i.e. alternative states) over time, but underlying environmental factors determining R&R typically experience little change. Therefore, use of landscape R&R indicators to characterize post-fire plant community composition at plot scales as in Applestein & Germino (2025) was inappropriate. The proximal environmental variables, climate and soil water availability, used to develop the landscape R&R indicators illustrated differences among ecoregions well, clearly separated R&R categories and were aligned with generalized ecological types ensuring broad-scale applicability. Use of distal proxies for environmental variables, like latitude and elevation, as in Applestein and Germino's study, provides limited insight into conditions that drive R&R across broad landscapes and over time. Landscape R&R indicators are predictive of generalized ecological types, ecosystem characteristics like productivity and plant functional types, and disturbance regimes. Refining these indicators may include identifying novel or finer scale explanatory environmental metrics generalizable in space and time, creating continuous indicators, or using higher resolution soil or climate data. Synthesis and applications. Landscape R&R indicators have performed well at large landscape scales and been used successfully to develop management strategies and prioritizations for the sagebrush biome and south-west drylands. Products derived from the indicators are being used to develop appropriate management strategies for large-scale planning areas. Appropriate use of the indicators, as shown here, requires understanding the relevant metrics and using properly scaled data.
